claim: The stem presupposes Chelsea won the PL under Mourinho, but Chelsea did not win the title in 2003-04 (Arsenal) or 2006-07 (Man Utd), so two of the four options are dismissible without knowing the points totals, leaving a 50/50 between 2004-05 and 2005-06.

Ferguson was Man Utd manager from November 1986 to May 2013 — 26 years and 6 months but 27 completed seasons — and both 26 and 27 are offered options, so the stem needs to say whether it means calendar years or seasons.

"How many Ballon d'Or awards has Messi won in total" has no "as of" qualifier (unlike q_816738 in the same batch), and the option list already contains 9, so the key silently rots if he ever wins another.
The stem's "teenage" qualifier eliminates all three distractors — Pedri (21), Gavi (20) and Bellingham (21) were all past their teens in 2024 — leaving Yamal as the only option that fits the stem.

Stem asks which club Haaland played for "before Manchester City" without saying "immediately before" — RB Salzburg (also an option) is likewise a club he played for prior to City, so a knowledgeable player can defensibly pick it and be marked wrong.
Sergio Ramos left Real Madrid for PSG in July 2021, so he fails the stem's own "for Real Madrid ... in the 2022 UCL semi-final" qualifier and can be dismissed without knowing the answer.

Benzema's tie-winning goal was a 95th-minute extra-time penalty, not a "last-minute winner" — the actual last-minute goals in that second leg were Rodrygo's 90' and 91' strikes, so the stem's description misstates the event it is testing.

q_a10f9b in the same bank ("Who scored 36 Premier League goals in 2022-23 to set a new single-season record?") states the numeric answer to this question, so the pair leaks into each other in any session that serves both.

The stem's "1978 World Cup winner" qualifier excludes all three distractors — Batistuta (b. 1969) and Crespo (b. 1975) were children in 1978 and Maradona was famously omitted from Argentina's 1978 squad — so Kempes is reachable without knowing the 'El Matador' nickname.

The stem's premise is false: 'Los Colchoneros' derives from Atletico's red-and-white striped shirts resembling the mattress ticking fabric of the era, not from any 'mattress-making sponsors' — the club never had such a sponsor. Keyed answer is still correct.

Mark Hughes also played Premier League football for Southampton (1998-2000) and Everton (2000), so the keyed pair 'Chelsea and Blackburn' is an incomplete answer to 'which other Premier League clubs' — a well-informed player may hesitate, though no other option is fully correct (option D pairs Everton with Tottenham, where he never played).

Mexico only leads on host count (1970, 1986, 2026) if its 2026 co-hosting with the USA and Canada is counted; on a sole-host reading Mexico ties Brazil, Italy and Germany on two, making three distractors equally defensible.

Wojciech Szczesny is Polish and was never in Italy's squad, so he fails the stem's 'for Italy' qualifier and is dismissible without knowing Donnarumma saved Saka's penalty (Sirigu and Meret were genuine Euro 2020 Italy keepers).

Cesc Fàbregas never played for Manchester United (Arsenal, Barcelona, Chelsea, Monaco), so he fails the stem's 'Manchester United legend' qualifier and can be dismissed without knowing the assists record.

The stem pins the season to 2022-23, but Andy Cole (retired 2008), Alan Shearer (retired 2006) and Luis Suárez (left the Premier League in 2014) were all out of the league by then, so every distractor fails the stem's own era qualifier.

Stem says "Champions League" but the keyed answer Matt Busby (1968) predates the 1992 rebrand; read literally the first manager to win the Champions League with an English club is Alex Ferguson (1999), who is not an option — the stem should say European Cup.

The stem pins the 2008-09 season, but Ibrahimović only joined Barcelona in summer 2009 and Villa in 2010, so two of the four options fail the stem's own era qualifier and can be dismissed without knowing the fact.

The count of men who have won the World Cup as both player and manager is currently three but is a live tally that changes with future tournaments; the "Four or more" option makes the rot explicit, and the correct option is also the only one that lists three names, a length/specificity tell.

RB Leipzig were in the third tier in 2011-12 (first promoted to the Bundesliga in 2016), so the distractor fails the stem's era without knowing the answer.

Mahrez was a Leicester player, never a manager, so the option fails the stem's 'who managed' qualifier and is dismissible without knowing Shakespeare.

The stem is written in future tense ('will host') but the 2026 World Cup concluded in July 2026, so the wording is already out of date.
Arsenal lead on FA Cups by a single title (14 v Man Utd's 13 after their 2024 win); one more Man Utd FA Cup makes two options equally correct.

The stem's arithmetic is wrong: Buffon's 17 Juventus seasons include 2006-07 in Serie B, so only 16 were top-flight (22 Italian top-flight seasons total by 2018, not 23) — the keyed club is still unambiguous.

The stem asks "What is the Derby della Madonnina" and then already answers that ("the famous Milan derby between Inter and AC Milan"), while the options actually answer a different question — the origin of the name — and the keyed option says "cathedral spire" when the derby is named after the Madonnina statue atop the Duomo's main spire.

The stem asks 'What is the fastest goal...' and then supplies the answer to its own question (8.3 seconds, San Marino v England 1993), while the four options are player names — it never actually asks who scored it.
'Man City' is listed as an option in a question asking which club beat Man City, so it fails the stem's own premise and can be dismissed immediately.
Stem is pinned to Euro 96, but distractors Rooney (born 1985) and Kane (born 1993) were children in 1996 and Lineker had retired in 1994, so three of four options fail the era qualifier.

'Six ever-present Premier League clubs' (Arsenal, Chelsea, Everton, Liverpool, Man Utd, Tottenham) is correct today but silently becomes wrong the season any of the six — Everton being the nearest risk — is relegated.
'As of 2026, most Champions League appearances' is a time-anchored record claim; the 'as of 2026' wording will read as outdated in later seasons even while Ronaldo's 183 remains the record.

'Win the World Cup as player and manager for the same country twice' does not parse cleanly — Zagallo won twice as a player but only once as a manager, so the 'twice' qualifier attaches to only half the clause and a reader could conclude no option fits.

Weah played for Chelsea (loan, early 2000) and then Manchester City (2000-01) before joining Marseille, so the qualifier 'before returning to France' actually points at Man City, not the keyed Chelsea.

Two distractors fail the stem's own qualifiers: Christian Vieri did not join Atlético Madrid until 1997 (so he was not there for the 1996 title), and José Luis Caminero was a midfielder, not a striker.
Platini (born 21 June 1955) played his final Juventus match on 17 May 1987, so he was 31 when he walked away, not the keyed 32 — the correct age is not among the options.
Michael Owen (born 1979) and Harry Kane (born 1993) could not have played at Mexico 1986, so two of the four options are dismissible on era alone without knowing the fact.
2016 is not a World Cup year, so that option can be eliminated by anyone who knows the four-year cycle, without knowing anything about Iceland.

The stem calls Watford a 'Premier League club', but Watford has been in the Championship since relegation in 2021-22, and Elton John's two chairmanships (1976-87, 1997-2002) largely predate or sit outside the club's PL spells; the descriptor will keep rotting with promotions/relegations.

'Longest-serving manager in English top-flight history' has no club/era qualifier and the superlative is contestable — George Ramsay ran Aston Villa 1884-1926 (~42 years, almost entirely First Division) and Fred Everiss was at West Brom 1902-48, both exceeding Ferguson's 26.5 years; the intended claim is presumably longest-serving at a single club in the Premier League era.

'Led Germany to the 2014 World Cup' reads as qualification rather than victory (the title word is missing); Löw is the answer under either reading, so nobody is misled, but the wording should be 'to the 2014 World Cup title'.

Distractor is spelled 'Raddy Antic'; the former Atlético manager is Radomir 'Radi' Antić — the misspelling (and the missing accents on 'Luis Aragones'/Aragonés) is inconsistent with other questions in the bank that use correct diacritics.

Shevchenko fails the stem's "Italian-based" qualifier for 1994-95 — he was at Dynamo Kyiv until 1999 and only joined Milan then, so he can be dismissed without knowing Batistuta won the 1994-95 Capocannoniere.

The record for scoring in most consecutive Champions League seasons (18, 2005-06 to 2022-23) is shared by Messi and Karim Benzema, so the singular 'which player ... the most' framing is inaccurate even though Benzema is not among the options.

'Most money across all career moves combined' is an unbounded career-aggregate superlative with no agreed methodology (loan fees, add-ons, and Neymar's disputed Santos fee all shift the total) and can change while Neymar and Mbappé are still transferable.

'What was the score before that miss?' can be read as the shootout tally (Brazil led 3-2 when Baggio stepped up) rather than the keyed 0-0 match score; only the fact that no option matches the shootout reading disambiguates it.

Eusébio scored four goals, not a hat-trick, in Portugal's 5-3 win over North Korea at the 1966 World Cup, so the stem understates the fact it is testing.

The stem's 'throughout his career' is false — Iniesta wore 34 on his 2002 debut and 24 the following season(s) before taking No. 8; the keyed '8' is right but the stem overstates.

"How many total has he won" is an open-ended present-tense count (currently three: 2015-16, 2016-17, 2020-21) that would silently become wrong if Kane, still an active player, returns to the Premier League and wins another Golden Boot.
